source.title: Index SLM Technical Report
source.authors: Lu-Sheng Zhang; Shien He; Tian-Xing Yan; Meng-Ran Yu; Ziang Cui; Kai Zhao; Xiaojing Liu; Tian-Jiao Li

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior claims about architecture shape but does not measure held-out loss across model sizes, tokens, or compute, fit scaling laws, or test compute-optimal allocations. Its depth comparison reports downstream benchmark scores rather than loss.
record.gate_note: The paper compares 36-layer and 9-layer models at fixed parameter count and reports benchmark scores across training. This is relevant to architecture shape but does not measure the loss named by V4. Other training-schedule and data ablations do not test the listed scaling-law versions. No cited results are recorded as this study's own findings.
record.test_reason: Section 6.2 sets Kaplan et al.'s weak-shape-dependence claim against Tay et al. It then compares 36-layer and 9-layer models at equal parameter count (1.01B non-embedding) and FLOPs. The outcome is average downstream benchmark score, not held-out pretraining loss, so it measures a related but different construct from V4. No loss-vs-scale fits, extrapolations, compute-optimal sweeps or downstream-vs-scale trends are reported. The other ablations (Norm-Head, learning rate, schedules, curated data, instruction data) also do not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report the deeper model is consistently better on average downstream score at equal size and FLOPs, and they adopt 36 layers. They add two caveats: depth raises activation memory, and the depth at which the benefit saturates is unknown.
record.recipe_differences: No scaling-law recipe is applied; this is a model-training and architecture ablation report.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture depth changes the reported downstream benchmark outcome in the fixed-parameter comparison; the text does not report exact values.

fits_no_version.finding: At 1.01B non-embedding parameters and equal FLOPs, the 36-layer model scores consistently above the 9-layer wider model on average benchmark score throughout 200–1000B tokens (Figure 3, figure-only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count and FLOPs, deeper-narrower small LMs reach higher downstream benchmark scores than shallow-wide ones.

record.problems: The architecture comparison's plotted benchmark values are not stated numerically in the text, and it reports benchmark scores rather than held-out loss. The authors also state that depth saturation has not been established.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were retained: the paper does not report results measuring the listed scaling-law versions. Other ablations, including learning-rate schedules and instruction-data mixtures, do not test those versions.

untested.parts: No held-out loss measured across parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
No compute-budget sweep or optimal parameter/token split.
Loss at fixed parameter count across shapes is not reported, only benchmark score. Only one depth pair (36 vs 9 layers) is tested.
No other modalities or regimes are fitted with power laws.
Benchmarks are tracked over training tokens for single runs, but no predictable relation to scale or loss is tested.
No exponents are fitted. The schedule comparison (Section 6.4) reports only that final validation losses converge, not scaling fits.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a model technical report. It cites Kaplan's shape claim but tests depth only on benchmark scores, so V4, which names loss, gets no verdict. A researcher may still treat Figure 3 as indirect, downstream-side tension with V4. Section 6.4 reports that validation losses for cosine, linear and WSD schedules converge to essentially the same final value on a 0.1B model trained on 1T tokens. That is not a scaling-law result and is not recorded as a row.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling of held-out pretraining loss with parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run scaling-law fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No compute-budget sweep or optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
Depth is compared at fixed parameter count, but the reported outcome is benchmark score, not held-out loss; the effects of width and other architecture details are not comprehensively tested.
No power-law test in other modalities or the listed training regimes.
Benchmark performance is reported, but no predictable relationship with scale or pretraining loss is tested.
No scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits are fitted or compared across setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: 36-layer configuration (1.01B non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean benchmark score with an equally sized 9-layer, wider model during training.
rows.measure: Average benchmark score (mean over C-Eval, CMMLU, MMLU, ARC-C, ARC-E, and HellaSwag)
rows.value: figure only; text says the deeper model is consistently better at equal size
rows.note: The reported comparison is about downstream benchmark score, not held-out loss; the text gives no exact score values.

rows.subject: 9-layer, wider counterpart (1.01B non-embedding parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Compared mean benchmark score with the 36-layer model at equal parameter count.
rows.measure: Average benchmark score (mean over C-Eval, CMMLU, MMLU, ARC-C, ARC-E, and HellaSwag)
rows.value: figure only; text says it is consistently below the deeper model at equal size
rows.note: The reported comparison is about downstream benchmark score, not held-out loss; the text gives no exact score values.
rows.check: R2 is the comparator arm of the same Figure 3 comparison as R1, not an independent result. It should serve as R1's baseline rather than a separate row. Values are figure-only: about 30–34 average score over 200–1000B tokens, with the deep curve above the wide one.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
